Stack tables one under the other

Source: R/table_stack.R
table_stack.Rd

table_stack() sets regression tables one under the other. Each table becomes a panel, opened by a row with its label, and keeps its own columns, rows, fit statistics and number formats: the cells of a panel have the content of the table passed, in every engine. The panels share one column header when they have the same columns, and each opens with its own header otherwise. Their notes are merged into one.

Build each table with its own arguments (vcov, cluster, exponentiate, p_adjust, show_columns, ...), then stack them: a grid of models is table_stack(table_regression(list(m1, m2)), table_regression(list(m3, m4))). For one panel per model of a list, table_regression(models, layout = "stacked") is the shortcut.

Usage

table_stack(
  ...,
  panel_labels = NULL,
  title = NULL,
  note = NULL,
  note_add = NULL,
  output = c("default", "data.frame", "long", "tinytable", "gt", "flextable", "excel",
    "clipboard", "word"),
  excel_path = NULL,
  excel_sheet = NULL,
  clipboard_delim = "\t",
  word_path = NULL,
  word_template = NULL
)

Arguments

...

Tables returned by table_regression() or table_regression_uv() with output = "default", one per panel, in the order of the panels. A name given here labels its panel: table_stack(Women = t1, Men = t2). A list of tables is spliced with !!!: table_stack(!!!tables).

panel_labels

Character vector, one non-empty label per table, in the order of the tables, unnamed: the labels of the panels not named in ... (a name given there takes precedence, with a warning). NULL (default) labels such a panel by the title you typed for its table, else by its outcome when the panels have different outcomes, else "Panel k". Two panels cannot share a label.

title

Title of the stacked table. NULL (default) keeps the title of the tables when they all have the same one, and gives none otherwise; FALSE gives none; a string sets it.

note

NULL (default) merges the notes of the panels; FALSE removes the note; a string replaces the general note, printed after the lead-in ("Note."), with the legend of the stars kept below it.

note_add

Sentences added at the end of the general note.

output

Output format, as in table_regression(): "default" (a printable data frame), "data.frame", "long", "tinytable", "gt", "flextable", "excel", "clipboard" or "word".

excel_path

File path for output = "excel", ending in ".xlsx", in a directory that exists. Default NULL (required when output = "excel").

excel_sheet

Sheet name when writing to Excel. NULL (the default) uses "Regression".

clipboard_delim

Field delimiter for output = "clipboard". Default "\t" (tab-separated, pastes cleanly into Excel / Google Sheets / Word). The clipboard payload mirrors the Excel layout (title row, spanner row, header, body, footer note) but is plain text – horizontal rules, cell merging, decimal alignment and the monospace font cannot be encoded in delimited text and are therefore absent from the paste. A cell holding the delimiter itself (a label with a comma under clipboard_delim = ",", or any number under decimal_mark = ","), a double quote or a line break is quoted RFC 4180-style, so the grid survives whatever delimiter you choose.

Paste behavior by target:

  • Excel / Google Sheets: numerics are auto-detected and right-aligned; text cells stay left-aligned. (P-values such as .005 get re-parsed as 0.005 by Excel's auto-format – to preserve the APA leading-zero-dropped display, prefer output = "excel".)

  • Word: the paste is converted to a Word table; all cells start left-aligned. Apply a Table Style (Insert > Table > Design) for APA-style borders, and set right-alignment on numeric columns (Layout > Align Right). For a self-contained Word file with borders and alignment pre-applied, use output = "word" instead.

word_path

File path for output = "word", ending in ".docx", in a directory that exists. Default NULL (required when output = "word"). The Word table inherits the flextable styling (Calibri font, APA borders, decimal-aligned numerics) and adds Word-specific features: an auto-numbered caption ("Table 1: ...", "Table 2: ...") via Word's SEQ field so multiple table_regression() calls in one document number consecutively; a re-printed header row on each page break; row split prevention so a single coefficient row never wraps across two pages; and an APA-styled note line (*Note.* italic prefix per APA Manual 7 §7.14).

R Markdown / Quarto: for embedded use, prefer output = "flextable" (returns the flextable object that knits to docx/HTML/PDF natively). output = "word" writes a standalone .docx file, suited to scripted exports rather than chunk-level rendering.

word_template

Optional path to a custom .docx file used as the template for output = "word". The template's header, footer, page size, margins, and named styles ("Table Caption" in particular) are honored; the table is appended to the template body. Useful for institutional templates with pre-set headers ("APA Style", "Manuscript Submission Template", etc.). Default NULL (uses flextable's stock template).

Customizing the caption appearance: the table caption is tagged with the Word named style "Table Caption". The visual rendering (italic / bold / color / font) follows whatever that style is set to in the docx template. The stock Word template renders "Table Caption" in italic — the APA Manual 7 §7.10 condensed convention. For a different appearance (Nature-style bold non-italic, APA-strict 2-line bold-number / italic-title, etc.), edit the "Table Caption" style in a docx template and pass it via word_template = "your_template.docx". Style-based delegation keeps the rendered caption consistent with the surrounding document and lets editorial conventions (Nature, APA-strict, journal-specific) be applied without modifying the call site.

Value

With output = "default", a spicy_stack_table (classes c("spicy_stack_table", "spicy_table", "data.frame")): the cells as printed, one row per printed row, plus a blank row for the bounds of an interval in a panel's header. Its attributes panels (the tables stacked, named by their labels), panel_rows (the rows of each panel in it, its label and header rows excluded), title and note are documented; the others are internal. as_structured() returns the typed views of the panels, as a named list.

With output = "data.frame" (and from as.data.frame()), the data frames of the panels bound by rows; with output = "long" (and from broom::tidy() and broom::glance()), the outputs of their models. Each opens with a panel column holding the label of the panel; the columns are the union of the panels' and the note, as printed, is the note attribute. In the output of table_stack(), a row is keyed by panel, model_id (the model inside its panel), term and estimate_type. With table_regression(layout = "stacked"), these three outputs are those of the same models side by side, panel aside: one row per (model_id, term, estimate_type), model_id being the identifier of the model in the list. With "tinytable", "gt" or "flextable", the object of that package; with "excel" or "word", the path of the file, invisibly; with "clipboard", the stacked table, invisibly.

Panels

A row with the label of the panel opens each panel ("Women:"), in the typography of the block headers. The label of a panel is its name in ..., else its entry in panel_labels, else the title you typed for its table (title = "..."), else its outcome when every panel has an outcome of its own, else "Panel k". A title spicy built is not a label: it describes the model ("Linear regression: bmi"), not the panel. The rows of a panel follow, in the order of its table: coefficients, blocks (thresholds, random effects, components), fit statistics.

When every panel has the same column headers, one header heads the whole table. Otherwise the header of the first panel heads it and each later panel opens with its own header rows, below its label row: an exponentiate = TRUE glm panel reads "OR" where an lm panel reads "B", and a multinomial panel keeps its outcome categories in columns. A panel narrower than the widest one leaves the extra columns blank. The header of a panel has the rows of the header of its table: its column groups, ruled under, its labels, and the bounds of its interval ("LL", "UL"), which the console leaves out since it prints an interval in one column.

In the console, the columns are matched by position and every panel shares their widths: a panel with other columns can widen a column of the first. When the panels have the same columns and decimals, the decimals line up from one panel to the next, only the padding of a cell changing; otherwise each panel keeps the padding of its table. When the console splits a wide stack by width, a column group cut by the split keeps its label over each part, and a continuation leaves out the panels with no cell in it. The other engines write each cell as its table does.

A table of table_regression_uv() is a panel like any other, its univariable models and their own sample sizes included.

Notes

The notes are merged sentence by sentence. The type of each model and its standard errors are worded as in a table of the models side by side: "Linear regression models.", or "Women: linear regression; Men: logistic regression." (in English; another language gives each panel its own sentence, as below), and "Std. errors: classical (OLS)." or one estimator per panel. So is an adjustment of the p-values ("P-values adjusted within each model ..."). Any other sentence that every panel carries is printed once, first; one that only some panels carry follows, opening with their labels ("Women, Men: ..."), panel after panel. The abbreviations are defined once. The legend of the stars is printed once, and when panels have different legends, each opens with the labels of its panels. A panel built with note = FALSE contributes no sentence, and one built with a typed note contributes that note.

Compatibility

The panels must be built in the same language (options(spicy.language)), with the same decimal_mark and align, and under styles that format a cell alike: the stacked table has one of each. Two styles that print the same table are compatible (no style and style = "apa"); a lever that differs (the decimals of a p-value, the separator or brackets of an interval, the minus sign, the lead-in of the note, the abbreviations) is not, nor is p_digits typed for one table of a theme that sets its own p-values. Otherwise table_stack() stops with spicy_stack_mismatch, naming what differs.

Only the tables of table_regression() and table_regression_uv() can be panels for now; the descriptive tables will follow.

Classed conditions

Errors carry spicy_invalid_input (no table, an object that is not a table built with output = "default", a stack passed as a panel, a table whose rows were changed after it was built, invalid or duplicated labels), spicy_empty_table (a table without rows), spicy_not_implemented with spicy_unsupported (a descriptive table) and spicy_stack_mismatch with spicy_invalid_input (panels built in different languages, with different decimal marks or alignments, or under styles that format a cell differently). Warnings carry spicy_ignored_arg (an entry of panel_labels overridden by a name in ...).

See also

table_regression(), whose layout = "stacked" stacks one panel per model; as_structured().

Examples

women <- sochealth[sochealth$sex == "Female", ]
men <- sochealth[sochealth$sex == "Male", ]
table_stack(
  Women = table_regression(lm(bmi ~ age + smoking, data = women)),
  Men = table_regression(lm(bmi ~ age + smoking, data = men))
)

# Panels with their own columns: the second opens with its header.
fit_bmi <- lm(bmi ~ age + sex, data = sochealth)
fit_dentist <- glm(dentist_12m ~ age + sex, data = sochealth,
                   family = binomial)
table_stack(
  BMI = table_regression(fit_bmi),
  Dentist = table_regression(fit_dentist, exponentiate = TRUE)
)
